title: Inference risk-reward sales brief: economics, fallback & objection scripts
content:
Purpose and scope:
Quick-use field brief for AEs and SEs to position Redwood vs general LLM API providers. Focus: communicating tradeoffs (latency vs cost), predictable economics (dedicated/reserved), and remediation when customers are seduced by lowest-cost-per-token pitches. Not a long deck—copyable talk tracks, demo checklist, and escalation triggers.

One‑liner positioning we want the rep to use:
"Redwood gives you predictable, production-grade inference across hosted, reserved, and private modes so you can ship features with reliable latency and unit economics — without re-architecting when usage spikes or regulatory needs arise."

Quick competitor framing (what customers hear):
- Generic LLM API vendors: "cheaper per token, always-on global API, limited SLA, model churn"
- Cloud-managed endpoints: "deep infra integration, complex ops, variable unit economics at scale"
- Self-hosted runtimes / OSS stacks: "full control, high ops burden, hidden performance tuning costs"

How Redwood contrasts (talk tracks):
- Predictable economics: reserved capacity and cost controls that let finance forecast spend (vs surprise token bills from bursty traffic).
- Production SLOs: latency & availability backed by dedicated capacity SLA or configurable fallbacks — sales-level reassurance for product teams.
- Unified developer experience: same API and rollout controls whether hosted, dedicated, or private — simplifies dev and QA.
- Cost-performance knobs: batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization profiles we recommend — cut unit costs without blind quality loss.
- Private & compliance ready: VPC and on-prem deployment options with KMS and audit log support — avoids last-mile security objections.

Competitor quick grid (cheat view to memorize):
- Model freshness: Competitors often claim newest models first; call out tradeoffs (unverified perf) and point to Redwood model catalog with verified performance profiles.
- Latency guarantees: Most LLM APIs offer best-effort; Redwood can offer dedicated SLOs and region routing.
- Predictability at scale: Third‑party APIs bill per token — show example math using customer traffic profile to expose unpredictability.
- Ops burden: Self-hosted = headcount + tuning. Redwood values: ops-light + tuning suggestions (Optimize).

Common customer objections and effective rebuttals:
1) "They are cheaper — why pay more?"
  - Rebuttal: "Ask how they handle 5x traffic spikes — do you get cost predictability, or will your cloud bill balloon? With Redwood reserved plans you get predictable committed cost and automatic fallback that avoids latency failures while keeping costs bounded. Want a quick number‑crunch for your traffic profile? I can run a model."
  - Demo artifact: cost-exemplar spreadsheet (linked) and quick calc cadence.

2) "We can self-host and save money."
  - Rebuttal: "Open-source stacks look cheap until you add SRE time, kernel tuning, quantization tradeoffs, and burst capacity. We published a post-mortem: self-hosted teams spend 3–6x more engineering time per month to reach reliable SLOs. If you want ownership, we offer private deployment and a handoff package so your infra team isn’t starting from scratch."

3) "We need the newest models immediately."
  - Rebuttal: "Redwood supports many models and verifies performance profiles; we can on-ramp new model variants behind flags with A/B rollout to protect quality. If wall‑clock novelty matters, we can map a staged play: quick-testing on hosted, then promote to dedicated as you validate."

4) "Latency is our top priority — some vendors advertise ultra-low latency."
  - Rebuttal: "Latency claims are often under constrained conditions. Redwood measures at token-level across realistic sequence lengths and offers dedicated pools with regional routing — let’s run a SLO-fit test against your 95th percentile latency target. If needed we’ll map fallback models to preserve availability under load."

Defensive probes to find competitive vulnerability:
- "How do you forecast monthly spend when traffic patterns are bursty?"
- "Who owns model rollouts and rollback in your current setup? How long to rollback a bad model?"
- "Do you have a documented latency SLO and an outage playbook for inference endpoints?"

Demo checklist (15-minute tradeoff demo flow):
1) Start with the customer scenario (volume, P95 target, regulatory constraints).
2) Show Redwood Console: per-route token cost, token-level latency breakdown, and a sample rollout where we flip from hosted to dedicated.
3) Walk the Optimize suggestions: batching profile change and quantization recommendation with estimated cost delta.
4) Run a quick failure scenario: region outage -> auto fallback to backup model/region and show alerting/tracing.
5) Share a short TCO calc for 6/12 months.

Traps and rebuttal playbook (things competitors will try):
- Pricing bait-and-switch: competitor offers $0.00X token to lock in POC — after 2–3 months they raise price or throttle. Response: show committed/burst blueprint and how Reserved plans prevent surprise throttles.
- Tech lingo confusion: some vendors will drown customers in model names/sizes. Response: translate to customer outcomes (tokens/sec, P95 latency, cost per successful call).
- Vendor lock threat: competitor claims their ecosystem makes migration costly. Response: emphasize Redwood’s unified API and model-version pinning — migration runway is shorter than they claim.

EScalation and win conditions for AE/SE:
- If customer cites complex compliance or on-prem needs, escalate to Solutions Engineering for private deployment sizing and a draft SOW.
- If cost is the only objection, request usage data and hand to Pricing for a reserved proposal.
- If latency is contested, schedule a short SLO-fit benchmark with the Benchmarks team (provide JIRA TBD).

One-page leave-behind bullets for execs:
- Predictable spend with Reserved + burst policies = finance-friendly
- Same API across hosted/dedicated/private = fewer dev regressions
- Backed by incident response and SLOs for production inference
- Cost controls: batching, caching, quantization advice tied to your evals

Open questions / doc TODOs (notes to SEs and product):
- Add region-specific latency numbers for dedicated SKUs (ask infra for updated table).
- Create a short scripted demo recording (1:30) showing failover flow.
- Build a one-click TCO calculator for common traffic shapes and attach to Console.

Useful quick links (for slides):
- Internal benchmark deck: confluence.redwood/internal/inference-economics-v2
- Cost exemplar spreadsheet: github.com/redwood-internal/cost-examples/blob/main/patterns.md

Notes to rep (quick copy/paste scripts):
- Opening: "One question before we start: if you could change one thing about your current model endpoint setup today, what would it be?"
- If stuck on price: "Let me map the numbers — 5 minutes of math beats 5 phone calls. Can you share a week of traffic?"
- Closing: "We can pilot a small slice on Hosted to validate quality, then move to Reserved when you want predictable economics. Usually customers see <90 days to baseline cost maturity."

Revision history: draft v0.9 — consolidated field feedback from Q4 pilots.
